A diskogram.

I have a herniated disk in my back, which created a sacral cyst, and eventually led to a fractured vertebrae. It's also causing nerve pressure, sporradically creating numbness and pain in my legs.

So, the doctors decided to do a diskogram, to determine exactly where that pressure was coming from, to determine how they'd treat my condition.

This was a procedure where they pulled out some fluorescent fluid, an X-ray machine, and a GIANT needle... They injected the fluid, directly into my spine (the herniated disk, and the disks above and below it, so three in total) so they could see it inflate on the X-ray. They would slowly inflate the disk, like a balloon, and continuously ask me what my pain level was, then continue to inject more fluid... Until I said I was at a 10 and couldn't take it any more.

I should also note that there was no anesthetic, since I had to "feel" where the pain was, so I could tell them what was causing my pain.

Then they said that I was to imagine that 10 was a 6, so we had "room" to move up and down... And they continued to inject fluid into my spine until I was at a 10 again...

At that point, they moved to the disk above, and repeated...

When they finished with the second disk, they "stabbed" round for the disk below, but couldn't find it... I don't remember that part, because I blacked it out of my memory. I just remember being driven home, in my car, and feeling EVERY bump in the road.

Eventually, I changed doctors, and the new one wanted to do the procedure himself... And I promptly told him i'd rather die.
Yeah.... Fuck that. I've been told I might need surgery in the future due to my herniated disks. But until they come up with a minimally invasive procedure I won't let any doc touch my spine.

They told me that I could have surgery, but the more research I did, the more I didn't want the surgery.

According to my research, and what the doctors told me (this was 5-10 years ago, just so you can guage things), there were only three types of surgery I could have received:

  1. Remove the problematic disc, then fuse the two vertabrae together. This will relieve the pressure on my nerve endings, but will limit my range of motion, due to literally losing a joint in my spine. Ultimately, this lack of motion will come back to bite me in the ass due to my young age. Essentially, the disks/joints above and below the fused joint will "overcompensate" for the missing disc... This will lead to both of them becomming inflamed, bulging, and eventually hanig to me removed... cascading into being in a wheelchair later on down the line.

  2. Remove the problematic disc, then replace it with an artificial disc. This seems like a good idea, until you learn that they hold the artificial disc in place with titanium rods, bolted to the vertebrae above and below the disc... sandwiching it into place... If this sounds like it'll limit your range of motion JUST LIKE fusing the two vertebrae together, that's because it does almost exactly that.

  3. Remove the problematic disc, then replace it with an experimental coil. This one was designed to NOT limit your range of motion, and relieve the pressure created by the problematic disc. The issue here is that it is (or was) a BRAND NEW procedure, so it hadn't been "tested" extensively, and my insurance wouldn't pay for any of it... and it was EXPENSIVE at the time.

So, ultimately, I opted for no surgery, and I decided to wait until I either got older or worse, to the point that I can't take the pain anymore. Hopefully, by that time, procedure #3 will be more viable, and I won't have to suffer for the rest of my life.
Hopefully there will be a 4th or 5th option by then...
